## Play it

[**Open the game →**](app/index.html) — bring your own OpenAI API key. It stays in
your browser and is sent directly to OpenAI; it never touches a server of mine.

## What this is

[Codenames Duet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codenames_(board_game)#Duet) is the
two-player, fully-cooperative variant of Codenames: instead of two teams racing each
other, you and a partner share the board and try to find all 15 of your agents
together before a shared 9-turn timer runs out. Each of you sees a key card the other
can't — so half the game is trusting a clue from someone who has information you
don't.

Here, the partner is an LLM. It takes turns being clue-giver (it can see its own key
card, and has to describe *its* agents without touching a bystander or the assassin)
and guesser (it sees only your clue and the board, and has to infer what you meant).

## The headline: getting *good* clues, not parsing text

The interesting problem here was never "get JSON out of the model." OpenAI's
[Structured Outputs](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/structured-outputs) mean
a response that matches a Zod schema is guaranteed — the model literally cannot return
malformed JSON. The actual work was making the *content* of that JSON good: clues a
human would find useful, and guesses that don't throw the game away on a hunch.

A few things did most of the work:

- **Role-specific system prompts.** Clue-giving and guessing are different jobs with
  different failure modes, so they get separate prompts (`CLUE_SYSTEM` /
  `GUESS_SYSTEM` in `src/prompts.ts`) rather than one prompt with a "you are either
  the giver or the guesser" branch. The clue-giver's prompt is explicit about the
  legality rules (one word, not on the board, count matches the target list) and
  about *strategy*: prefer a clue that safely covers a couple of agents over an
  ambitious one that risks pointing at a bystander or the assassin.
- **A worked example, right in the system prompt.** Rather than describing the output
  format abstractly, the clue prompt includes one concrete board → clue → reasoning
  example. Cheap to write, and it does more for output quality than another paragraph
  of rules.
- **Reasoning before the answer.** Both schemas put a free-text `reasoning` field
  first, ahead of `clue`/`targets` or `guesses`. Structured Outputs fills fields in
  order, so this forces the model to work out *why* before it commits, instead of
  pattern-matching straight to an answer and rationalizing it afterward.
- **Steering away from the assassin explicitly**, not just implicitly through "be
  careful." The rules block repeats it up front (the assassin ends the game
  instantly; a bystander just burns the turn) and the strategy line names the tradeoff
  by name, because "give a safe clue" without saying what "unsafe" costs is exactly
  the kind of guidance a model will silently discount.
- **Compact, cache-first prompts.** Every clue/guess request sends the same static
  system message followed by a user message built from the current board and turn
  history (`buildClueMessages` / `buildGuessMessages`). Nothing in the system prompt
  changes turn-to-turn, which is what OpenAI's prompt caching needs to actually kick
  in — and it also just keeps the prompt small.

None of that is verifiable by reading the prompt, though — clue quality is an
empirical claim, so it's measured, not asserted.

### Results (from a local eval run)

`eval/run.ts` plays the AI against itself — both clue-giver and guesser — for *N*
full games and reports aggregate quality metrics: win rate, average agents found,
how often it hit the assassin, the illegal-clue rate (before repair), and repairs per
clue. It's a dev-only harness (`npm run eval`), never run in CI or tests, because it
spends real OpenAI credits.

To reproduce, from `codenames/`:

```bash
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... npm run eval -- 20
```

**To be filled in from a local run** — I haven't spent the API budget to generate

## Architecture: a static site with no backend

This whole project is static files served by GitHub Pages — the same as the rest of
this site. There's no server that talks to OpenAI on the user's behalf, which means
no server holding an API key, no server bill, and no server to maintain. It also
means the browser calls OpenAI's API directly, which the `openai` SDK doesn't do by
default — it's built assuming a trusted backend and refuses to run in a browser
unless you pass `dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true`.

That flag name is doing its job: it's an honest tradeoff, not a workaround. Bring
your own key, and it stays yours — it's read into memory (optionally cached in
`sessionStorage`, never `localStorage`, never logged), used for calls straight from
your browser to OpenAI, and gone when the tab closes unless you asked it to
remember. The alternative — a small proxy server that holds a shared key — would
mean I'm paying for (and rate-limiting, and securing) everyone's games instead of
each player paying for their own. For a hobby project, "no server" beats "my server,
my API bill" every time.

## Token cost

Ballpark, a full game costs somewhere around **$0.005–$0.08**, depending on model and
how many turns it takes to finish — call it somewhere between a dozen and a couple
hundred games per dollar (reasoning models cost more, since you pay for the hidden
thinking). The system prompts are static (helping prompt caching) and responses are
capped at 8192 completion tokens — high because reasoning models spend hidden
reasoning tokens against that same budget, while the actual JSON answer is tiny.

## Interpret → validate → repair

Because Structured Outputs guarantees schema-valid JSON, "parsing the response" was
never the hard part. The hard part was that schema-valid isn't the same as
*legal* — the model can return perfectly well-formed JSON that breaks a game rule:
a clue that's two words, a clue that's a word already on the board, a `number` that
doesn't match the length of `targets`, a target that isn't actually one of its own
remaining agents. `validateClue` in `src/validate.ts` checks all of that after the
schema already passed.

When a clue fails validation, `getAIClue` doesn't just discard it — it appends the
bad response and a repair message (`repairMessage`, naming the specific violations)
to the conversation and asks again, up to `MAX_REPAIRS` (2) times, before giving up
and passing the turn. Guesses get a lighter touch: `filterGuesses` just silently
drops any guessed word that isn't actually still on the board, since a guess can't
break the game the way an illegal clue can.

The other failure modes weren't about content at all:

- **Truncation** — if the model gets cut off before finishing the JSON, the SDK's
  `parse()` throws (there's no half-object to hand back). Reasoning models made this
  real: their hidden thinking counts against the token budget, so a too-small cap
  truncates before the answer. The fix is mostly prevention — a generous 8192-token
  budget — and if it still happens it's mapped to a typed `LLMError` and surfaced in
  the UI with a Retry button rather than silently retried.
- **Refusals** — Structured Outputs can return a `refusal` field instead of
  `parsed`. Treated as "pass the turn," logged, not retried.
- **Auth and rate limits** — a 401 or 429 from the API is caught and turned into a
  typed `LLMError` (`kind: "auth" | "rate_limit" | "network" | "other"`) so the UI can
  show something actionable ("bad key" vs. "slow down") instead of a raw stack trace.

So the pipeline is really interpret (schema, guaranteed) → validate (semantic
legality, the actual work) → repair (bounded retry with the specific violation fed
back), and everything below that is ordinary API-failure handling.

## A design cut: no sudden death

Real Codenames Duet has a sudden-death round if you run out of turns with a partial
board: you keep going with harsher rules until someone wins or hits a bystander/the
assassin. I cut it. Sudden death only makes sense if both players can keep playing
normally, and the AI here has no notion of "I'm out of good clues, but I have to say
*something* anyway" — every clue it gives already reflects its best guess about the
current board, timer or no timer. Bolting a special extra-harsh mode onto a
partner that doesn't have a concept of desperation would have been a lot of code to
implement something the AI couldn't meaningfully play differently. So the rule here
is simpler than the physical game's: run out the 9 turns without finding all 15
agents, and it's a loss.
